Below is a consolidated, coach‑ready, full 12‑week program for your client: a 58‑year‑old male, 6 months post‑MI, cleared for moderate intensity only, HR target ≲115 bpm (~70% age‑predicted max) unless cardiology gives different limits, no Valsalva, no maximal lifts. It integrates the cardiac‑safe aerobic progression (higher volume for weight loss), increased strength emphasis with compound lifts (safe variations: goblet, box/safety‑bar, trap‑bar, RDL, kettlebell), the nutrition plan previously provided (heart‑healthy, mild calorie deficit, protein 1.0–1.2 g/kg), option to introduce very conservative HIIT only with cardiology clearance, and builds to a supervised 5K time trial in Week 12 if cleared.

Before you use the plan — must reads
- Medical clearance: continue coordination with cardiologist/cardiac rehab. Obtain explicit written clearance before attempting higher‑effort intervals, HIIT, or the 5K time trial.
- Monitoring: client must wear a reliable HR monitor (chest strap preferred). If on beta‑blockers, HR will be blunted — use RPE primarily (target RPE 11–13; brief up to 14 if physician approves).
- Symptoms: stop and follow emergency protocol for chest pain, severe breathlessness, syncope, new palpitations, or dizziness.
- Breathing: no Valsalva. Teach diaphragmatic breathing and exhale on exertion; keep loads submaximal and avoid training to failure.
- Supervision & equipment: supervise heavier compound lifts initially; have AED and emergency plan accessible.

Structure summary
- Duration: 12 weeks, 3 supervised strength sessions/week (Mon/Wed/Fri) + 2 dedicated cardio sessions/week (Tue/Sat) + 1 active recovery day + daily walks/NEAT as tolerated.
- Strength focus: compound lifts included and progressed safely (goblet squat → box/safety bar → box or safety-bar squats; RDL → trap‑bar deadlift; step‑ups, Bulgarian split, hip thrusts). Working rep ranges are conservative: early higher reps (10–15), then shift to 6–10 reps for strength progression; keep RPE ≤13.
- Cardio focus for weight loss: weekly cardio minutes increased progressively to ~200–250 min/week by mid-late program, relying on steady‑state and controlled intervals (not all‑out HIIT). HIIT only if cardiologist clears — a conservative intro is described but not required.
- 5K time trial: planned for end of Week 12 only with explicit medical clearance and supervised testing. If not cleared, use 6‑minute walk test or a controlled 2 km brisk walk test as alternatives.
- Nutrition: heart‑healthy Mediterranean/DASH pattern, sodium 1,500–2,000 mg/day, protein ~1.0–1.2 g/kg/day, mild caloric deficit ~300–500 kcal/day for weight loss; details and meal examples from prior guidance.

Weekly microstructure & progression
- Weeks 1–4 Phase 1 (Reconditioning & movement/technique)
  - Focus: movement quality, breathing, introduce compound patterns, build baseline aerobic capacity.
  - Strength plan: 2–3 sets per exercise; rep ranges 12–15 → 10–12; emphasis on goblet squat, kettlebell deadlift, RDL variations, box squat; machine/chest‑supported upper work.
  - Cardio: build to 120–150 min/week total aerobic minutes. Two longer walks (30–45 min) + short 10–20 min post strength sessions.
  - Strength sessions emphasize technique, tempo 2:2, rests 60–120s.
  - Nutrition: start calorie deficit if safe, distribute protein across meals, implement sodium reduction strategies.

- Weeks 5–8 Phase 2 (Build submaximal strength & aerobic capacity)
  - Focus: increase strength volume and load conservatively; introduce trap‑bar deadlift and heavier RDLs; increase aerobic minutes.
  - Strength plan: main lifts 3–4 sets; rep ranges 8–10 (primary) and 6–8 for heavier work later; rest 90–150s. Compound list: trap‑bar deadlift, box/safety‑bar squat or heavy goblet, Bulgarian split squat, seated presses/rows for upper body.
  - Cardio: increase to ~160–200 min/week. One longer steady session 45–55 min; one interval session (moderate intervals 3 min work/2 min recovery) 30–40 min; short steady cardio after strength (20–25 min).
  - Nutrition: maintain deficit with higher protein (~1.0–1.2 g/kg), post‑workout protein snack; track sodium, fiber, healthy fats.

- Weeks 9–12 Phase 3 (Consolidation: functional strength, higher cardio volume, 5K prep and conservative HIIT option)
  - Focus: consolidate strength gains with submaximal heavier sets and functional carries; cardio volume peaks for weight loss; begin 5K prep week 9–12 and conservative intro to HIIT only if cleared.
  - Strength plan: main lifts 3–4 sets × 6–8 reps for trap‑bar deadlift, box/safety‑bar squat, RDL; include carries, step ups, hip thrusts. Avoid 1RM testing; keep RPE ≤13.
  - Cardio: target 200–250 min/week with two longer sessions (50–60 min steady + 30–45 min interval-style moderate session). Short cardio after strength sessions (20–25 min) continues.
  - 5K prep: a structured 4‑week build (Weeks 9–12) leading to a supervised 5K time trial on Week 12 if cardiology clears. If not cleared, substitute a 6‑minute walk test or 2 km brisk walk.
  - HIIT option: conservative introduction (30–45s work/90–120s recovery, on recumbent bike or elliptical) starting only after written clearance and >8 weeks symptom‑free. Supervise all initial HIIT sessions and document response.
  - Nutrition: maintain deficit, monitor weight weekly, ensure adequate protein and hydration; adjust calories if weight loss stalls.

Detailed week‑by‑week summary (sessions and key exercises)
Notation: sets × reps. Rest = recommended rest between working sets. Keep tempo controlled (approx 2s concentric : 2–3s eccentric). Abbreviations: RPE = rate of perceived exertion.

Phase 1 — Weeks 1–4 (reconditioning)
Week 1 (example)
- Mon — Strength A (Lower focus) ~50–60 min
  - Warm‑up 8–10 min (bike/walk + mobility)
  - Goblet squat 2 × 12–15 (rest 90s)
  - Kettlebell deadlift 2 × 12–15 (90s)
  - Box squat (bodyweight or light DB) 2 × 10–12 (90s)
  - Split‑stance RDL 2 × 10 each leg (60–90s)

  - Seated DB overhead press (light) 2 × 10–12

  - Seated DB overhead press 3 × 8–10

- Fri — Strength C (Full body/unilateral) ~60 min
  - Trap‑bar or kettlebell deadlift 3 × 6–8
  - Step‑ups with DB 3 × 8–10 each
  - Lat pulldown or pull‑up progression 3 × 8–10
  - Dumbbell bench press 3 × 8–10

Compound lifts & progression specifics (safe variants and loads)
- Use goblet squat → box/safety-bar squat → (only if cleared) light barbell squat. Work sets progress from 12–15 reps → 8–10 → 6–8. Keep 2–3 reps in reserve (RPE ≤13).
- Use kettlebell deadlift → RDL → trap‑bar deadlift. Prefer trap‑bar for heavier work because of more upright posture and easier breathing. Avoid conventional heavy barbell deadlifts unless technique and medical clearance are excellent.
- Warm‑up sets: 2–3 ramping warm sets before heavy compound sets (light → medium).
- Load increases: small increments (2.5–5% upper body, 5–10% lower body) when client completes top of rep range with RPE ≤12 and HR remains safe.
- Rest: 90–180s between heavy compound sets. Longer rest allows HR to fall and reduces hemodynamic strain.
- Breathing cue: inhale to prepare, brace lightly, exhale on concentric effort. Practice bracing without prolonged breath holding; reduce load if needed.

- Primary HR cap ≲115 bpm unless cardiologist prescribes another limit. If on beta‑blocker, use RPE 11–13 as primary intensity measure.
- Cardio modalities: brisk walking with incline, recumbent bike, elliptical, swimming/water walking (good for high minutes and low impact).
- Steady sessions: 45–60 min at RPE 11–13. Interval sessions: moderate intervals (e.g., 3 min work / 2 min easy) with careful HR monitoring. HIIT only if cleared and introduced conservatively (short bursts 30–45s with long recoveries).
- Weekly progression: aim to reach ~200–250 min/week by Weeks 8–10 for weight loss, then maintain.

Nutrition reminders (apply throughout 12 weeks)
- Calorie target: create a moderate deficit ~300–500 kcal/day from estimated maintenance. If you want a precise calorie target, give current weight — I can calculate.
- Protein: ~1.0–1.2 g/kg/day (spread 20–30 g per meal). Older clients and those doing strength need adequate protein.
- Sodium: aim ~1,500–2,000 mg/day unless physician advises otherwise.
- Meal timing: small carb + protein snack pre/post‑workout (e.g., banana + 10–20 g protein) to support recovery and training.
- Hydration, fiber (25–35 g/day), healthy fats (olive oil, nuts), 2 servings/week fatty fish.

Monitoring, reassessment & safety checkpoints
- Baseline measures (before starting): resting HR & BP, medication list, 6‑minute walk test or baseline 2 km/5 min walk pace, baseline strength (submaximal e.g., 8RM estimates for trap‑bar or goblet), bodyweight, and symptom history.
- Reassess at weeks 4, 8 and 12: vitals, functional tests (6MWT or 2 km), weight, and strength progression logs.
- Document HR and RPE for each session; log any symptoms. Share with cardiologist if requested.
- Stop and evaluate if resting BP or HR is out of expected range, or if client experiences concerning symptoms during or after sessions.

Alternatives if not cleared for 5K or HIIT
- 6‑minute walk test or 2 km brisk walk test are safer performance endpoints.
- Focus on steady state cardio volume for weight loss and strength improvements without maximal efforts.

Practical notes for you the trainer
- Supervise the first 2–3 heavy compound sessions closely; practice breathing/bracing drills before adding load.
- Use machines and supported positions for early heavy sets (leg press, seated chest press) if breathing or balance is a concern.
- Keep sessions flexible: if HR drifts up across a session, reduce loads, shorten cardio, extend rests, or switch to a recumbent modality.
- Use RPE and symptoms when HR is unreliable (beta‑blocker).

If you want next steps

- I can calculate a precise calorie target and provide 2 week sample meal plans and grocery lists if you give current weight and target weight loss rate.

High‑Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) can produce superior cardiovascular and metabolic adaptations and aid weight loss, but in a post‑MI client you must balance benefits against safety risks (arrhythmia, ischemia, blood pressure spikes). Below I outline a safe pathway to introduce HIIT‑style work in later phases (weeks 9–12 or beyond) if and only if all of the following are true:

Required prerequisites (all must be satisfied)
- Explicit medical clearance from his cardiologist or cardiac rehabilitation team to perform higher‑intensity intervals beyond moderate intensity.
- Stable clinical status: no recent angina, no uncontrolled hypertension, no decompensated heart failure, no concerning arrhythmias, and stable medication regimen.
- Consistent tolerance of the current program: at least 8–10 weeks of the progressive program completed with no cardiac symptoms, with resting BP and HR stable, and good recovery (normal HR recovery 3–5 min post‑exercise).
- He understands and accepts the increased perceived exertion and risk; sessions are supervised by you (trainer) with immediate access to emergency procedures (AED, phone, staff).
- Preferably not on medications or conditions that make intensity unpredictable; if he is on beta‑blockers, HIIT’s HR targets are unreliable — use RPE carefully and be more conservative.

If cleared, how to introduce HIIT safely (progression and limits)
1) Use a conservative definition of HIIT: intervals that elevate RPE to 13–15 briefly but keep HR below or near the clinic limit (ideally still ≤115 bpm unless cardiology allows a higher cap). If HR is unreliable (beta‑blocker), rely on RPE and symptoms.
2) Start with low‑impact modalities where workload and intensity can be precisely controlled and stopped quickly: recumbent bike, rowing ergometer, elliptical, or pool (aqua intervals). Avoid treadmill sprints or high‑impact plyometrics.
3) Supervise all initial HIIT sessions in person. Keep emergency equipment and protocols in place.
4) Use short work intervals and long recoveries initially, and progress only if well tolerated.

Sample conservative HIIT progression (to consider starting in Weeks 9–12 only after clearance)

Stage 1 — Introductory “controlled higher effort” (Week 9–10)
- Modality: recumbent bike or elliptical (easier to monitor, less orthostatic stress).
- Session structure (start with 1 session/week replacing one moderate cardio session):
  - Warm‑up: 10 min easy.
  - Work: 6 × (30–45 seconds higher effort / 90–120 seconds easy recovery). Higher effort should feel like RPE 13–14 (somewhat hard to hard). Aim to keep HR below prescribed cap (115 bpm) — if HR rises too high, reduce resistance or shorten work time.
  - Cool down: 8–10 min easy.
- Rationale: very short bursts limit hemodynamic stress while providing stimulus for fitness.

Stage 2 — Moderate interval progression (Week 11)
- If Stage 1 well tolerated and cardiologist OK, progress to:
  - 5–6 × (60 seconds moderate‑high effort / 120–180 seconds easy). RPE target 13–14. Monitor HR and symptoms closely.
  - Keep session frequency at 1×/week supervised; continue other moderate cardio sessions for total weekly volume.

Stage 3 — Slightly longer intervals (Week 12+ only if cleared and tolerated)
- Progress to no more than 2 HIIT sessions/week, and only if all signs remain benign:
  - 4–6 × (90 seconds higher effort / 2–3 minutes easy). RPE 13–14; if HR allowed by cardiologist, peaks may approach but not exceed physician-set limit.
- Maintain at least 48 hours between HIIT sessions and avoid pairing HIIT with heavy resistance sessions the same day.

Ongoing safety measures for HIIT
- Continuous HR monitoring and RPE check every interval; ask for symptom check each recovery period.
- Keep intervals conservative in duration and intensity; emphasize controlled breathing, avoid Valsalva, and discourage maximal pushing to failure.
- Avoid warm weather or dehydration that can increase cardiac strain during HIIT.
- Use seated or supported positions for resistance if HIIT includes strength components.
- If on beta‑blockers: use RPE-based cues (13–14 max) and avoid HR reliance.
- Ensure rapid cool‑down to prevent post‑exercise hypotension or arrhythmia — 8–10 min low effort after intervals.

Alternative (lower‑risk) high‑effort options
- Aerobic interval training with sustained moderate intervals (4 min moderate / 2 min easy) — sometimes called “submaximal interval training” — provides many HIIT benefits with lower risk than all‑out sprints.
- Aqua intervals (pool): allow safe higher perceived effort with reduced orthostatic and impact stress.
- Incline walking intervals: increase grade rather than speed — easier to control intensity and slower muscle actions reduce Valsalva.

Decision algorithm for you (trainer)
- If cardiology clearance = No → do not perform HIIT; continue higher-volume moderate cardio and strength-based weight loss strategy.
- If cardiology clearance = Conditional (higher HR cap or specific protocol) → follow cardiologist’s exact parameters for HR/RPE and monitor closely.
- If clearance = Yes and client tolerant for 8–10 weeks → begin Stage 1 HIIT under supervision, review symptom log and vitals after first 2–3 sessions, then decide progression.

When to stop HIIT immediately
- Any chest pain, new or worsening angina, syncope/lightheadedness, palpitations with hemodynamic instability, severe shortness of breath, or HR above physician’s limit during or after intervals.
- New arrhythmias noted on monitoring, or abnormal BP response (excessive rise or fall) — stop and seek medical evaluation.

- Keep overall weekly energy expenditure similar; if HIIT increases cardiac stress, reduce total weekly interval volume or replace another session with active recovery.

- Document cardiology clearance in writing and keep it in his file.

- Reassess after 2–4 supervised HIIT sessions and consult the cardiac team if anything abnormal appears.
